questions.stem: What two parts make up the German perfect tense?
options: A modal verb and an infinitive
An auxiliary verb and a past participle
questions.explanation: „Haben“ or „sein“ in the present, plus a participle at the end of the clause: „ich habe gespielt“, „ich bin gegangen“. It is the tense Germans use for most spoken past.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary do most German verbs take in the perfect tense?
questions.explanation: Most take „haben“. Verbs of movement and change of state take „sein“ — „ich bin gefahren“, „ich bin geblieben“ — which is a short list worth memorising.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „spielen“?
questions.explanation: Regular verbs form the participle with ge- … -t. „Spielte“ is the simple past, used more in writing than in speech.

questions.stem: Where does the past participle go in a main clause?
questions.explanation: „Ich habe gestern Fußball gespielt“ — the auxiliary is second and the participle is last, with everything else in between. German brackets the sentence between two halves of the verb.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary does „gehen“ take in the perfect tense?
questions.explanation: „Gehen“ is a verb of movement, so „ich bin gegangen“. Using „haben“ here is the commonest error for English speakers, who have only one auxiliary to choose from.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I drove to Berlin yesterday'?
options: Ich bin gestern gefahren nach Berlin
Ich gefahren bin gestern nach Berlin
Ich bin gestern nach Berlin gefahren
Ich habe gestern nach Berlin gefahren
questions.explanation: „Fahren“ takes „sein“, and the participle goes last — after the time and the place. German orders that middle section time, manner, place.

questions.stem: In „Ich helfe dem Mann“, why is it „dem“?
questions.explanation: A small group of verbs — helfen, danken, folgen, gefallen — take the dative where English would use a direct object. There is no logic to recover; they are learned as a list.

questions.stem: Which case follows „mit“?
questions.explanation: „Mit“ is always dative: „mit dem Bus“, „mit meiner Schwester“. Aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu is the set worth learning as a chant.

questions.stem: Which case follows „für“?
questions.explanation: „Für“ is always accusative: „für meinen Bruder“. Für, um, durch, gegen, ohne is the matching set on the other side.

questions.stem: What does the modal verb „müssen“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Müssen“ is obligation, „dürfen“ is permission and „können“ is ability. English 'must not' and German „muss nicht“ are false friends: „muss nicht“ means 'doesn't have to'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I can speak German'?
questions.explanation: A modal verb takes second position and sends the other verb to the end as an infinitive. English keeps the two verbs together, which is the habit the wrong options show.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I think that he is coming tomorrow'?
options: Ich denke, dass er kommt morgen
Ich denke, dass kommt er morgen
Ich denke, dass er morgen kommen
Ich denke, dass er morgen kommt
questions.explanation: „Dass“ is a subordinating conjunction, so the verb goes to the very end of its clause. The comma before it is compulsory in German, unlike English.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'when I was young, I played football'?
options: Als ich jung war, ich habe Fußball gespielt
Wenn ich jung war, habe ich Fußball gespielt
Als ich jung war, habe ich Fußball gespielt
Als ich war jung, habe ich Fußball gespielt
questions.explanation: Two rules at once: „als“ sends its verb to the end, and the main clause then starts with its verb because the subordinate clause occupies first position. „Als“ is for a single past period; „wenn“ would mean 'whenever'.

questions.stem: In „Ich stelle das Glas auf den Tisch“, why is it „den Tisch“?
options: The verb is in the past
There is movement onto the table, so it takes the accusative
questions.explanation: „Auf“ is a two-way preposition: accusative for movement towards, dative for position. „Auf dem Tisch“ would mean the glass is already there.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I would like to go to Germany'?
options: Ich will nach Deutschland fahren gern
questions.explanation: „Nach“ is used for countries and cities without an article; „zu“ is for people and specific places. The infinitive goes last, after the destination.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the man whose car is red'?
options: der Mann, dessen Auto rot ist
der Mann, wessen Auto rot ist
der Mann, dessen Auto ist rot
der Mann, der Auto rot ist
questions.explanation: „Dessen“ is the masculine genitive relative pronoun. The verb still goes to the end of the relative clause, which is what the third option gets wrong.

questions.stem: What is the difference between „kennen“ and „wissen“?
options: „Kennen“ is knowing a person or place; „wissen“ is knowing a fact
questions.explanation: English uses 'know' for both. „Ich kenne Berlin“ but „ich weiß, wo Berlin ist“ — and „wissen“ is irregular, giving „ich weiß“ rather than 'ich wisse'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been learning German for two years'?
options: Ich habe seit zwei Jahren Deutsch gelernt
Ich lerne für zwei Jahre Deutsch
Ich lernte seit zwei Jahren Deutsch
Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch
questions.explanation: German keeps the present tense with „seit“ when something is still going on, exactly as French does with „depuis“. „Seit“ also takes the dative, which is why it is „zwei Jahren“.

questions.stem: Which case does the preposition "mit" always take?
questions.explanation: Mit is a dative preposition, so it is always followed by dem, der or den plus n. Learning the dative prepositions as a list is faster than deciding each time.

questions.stem: Complete: Ich fahre ___ dem Bus.
questions.explanation: Mit dem Bus is the standard way to say by bus, and mit takes the dative, which dem shows. Für, ohne and durch all take the accusative.

questions.stem: Which sentence puts the verb in the right place?
questions.explanation: The finite verb is always the second element in a main clause, so putting morgen first pushes the subject after the verb. This inversion is the rule that most often trips up English speakers.

questions.stem: Where does the verb go in a clause beginning with "weil"?
questions.explanation: Weil is a subordinating conjunction, and it sends the finite verb to the end of its clause. Denn means the same thing but leaves the word order alone.

questions.stem: Complete: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank ___.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with ich, so it is bin, and weil sends it to the end. Both the agreement and the position have to be right.

questions.stem: Which is the perfect tense of "Ich spiele Fußball"?
questions.explanation: Spielen takes haben as its auxiliary and forms a regular past participle with ge and t. The last option is the simple past, not the perfect.

questions.stem: Which verb takes "sein" in the perfect tense?
questions.explanation: Verbs of motion and change of state take sein. Gehen, fahren, kommen and bleiben are the ones met most often at this level.

questions.stem: Complete: Er ___ nach Berlin gefahren.
questions.explanation: Fahren is a verb of motion, so it takes sein rather than haben. Using hat here is the single most common perfect-tense error.

questions.stem: What is the accusative form of "der Hund"?
questions.explanation: Only the masculine changes in the accusative, from der to den. Feminine, neuter and plural look the same as the nominative.

questions.stem: Complete: Ich sehe ___ Mann.
questions.explanation: The man is the object of sehen, so it takes the accusative, and masculine accusative is den. Identifying who does the action decides the case.

questions.stem: Which modal verb means "to be allowed to"?
questions.explanation: Dürfen is permission and können is ability, and the two are easily confused. Müssen is necessity and sollen is obligation or advice.

questions.stem: Where does the infinitive go in "Ich muss meine Hausaufgaben machen"?
options: At the start of the clause
At the end of the clause
questions.explanation: A modal verb sends the second verb to the end in its infinitive form. The bracket this creates around the sentence is a defining feature of German.

questions.stem: What is the comparative of "gut"?
questions.explanation: Gut is irregular, becoming besser and then am besten. Regular adjectives simply add er.

questions.stem: Complete: Mein Bruder ist ___ als ich.
questions.explanation: A comparison between two people needs the comparative with als. The superlative would be used only for three or more.

questions.stem: Which word order is correct: time, manner, place?
options: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Wien
Ich fahre nach Wien morgen mit dem Zug
Ich fahre mit dem Zug morgen nach Wien
Ich fahre nach Wien mit dem Zug morgen
questions.explanation: German orders adverbials as time, then manner, then place, which is the reverse of the usual English order. Getting it wrong is understandable but marked.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "das Buch"?
questions.explanation: Many neuter nouns add er and take an umlaut in the plural, and every plural takes die. German plurals have to be learned with the noun.

questions.stem: Complete: Wenn ich Zeit ___, würde ich mehr lesen.
questions.explanation: This is a conditional, so it needs the subjunctive hätte rather than the indicative habe. Wenn also sends the verb to the end.

questions.stem: What does "seit" tell you about the tense used?
options: German uses the present for something still going on
German uses the perfect, like English
questions.explanation: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier means I have lived here for three years. German keeps the present because the action continues.

questions.stem: Which pronoun replaces "dem Lehrer"?
questions.explanation: Dem shows the dative, and the masculine dative pronoun is ihm. Ihn would be accusative and er nominative.

questions.stem: Why do the two-way prepositions take two cases?
options: Accusative is formal and dative informal
Accusative is singular and dative plural
The case depends on the gender of the noun
Accusative shows movement, dative shows position
questions.explanation: In, an, auf and the rest take the accusative when the phrase answers wohin and the dative when it answers wo. Movement against location is the whole test.

questions.stem: Complete: Das Buch liegt ___ dem Tisch.
questions.explanation: Liegen describes position rather than movement, so the two-way preposition takes the dative, shown by dem. Legen would describe placing it there and take the accusative.

questions.stem: What is the German for "I would like"?
questions.explanation: Möchte is the polite way to ask for something in a shop or a restaurant. Ich will is much more direct and can sound rude.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „machen“?
questions.explanation: Weak verbs take ge- plus the stem plus -t. Strong verbs take ge- plus a changed stem plus -en, as in „gesungen“.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „sehen“?
questions.explanation: „Sehen“ is strong, so it keeps -en and changes nothing else. „Sah“ is the imperfect, a different tense entirely.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „trinken“?
questions.explanation: Strong verbs often change their stem vowel in the participle: trinken, trank, getrunken. The three forms are learnt as a set.

questions.stem: Why does „besuchen“ have no ge- in its participle?
options: It takes sein in the perfect
It begins with an inseparable prefix
questions.explanation: Verbs starting be-, ver-, er-, ent-, emp- or zer- never add ge-, giving „besucht“ and „verstanden“. Verbs ending -ieren skip it too.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „studieren“?
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge-. They are nearly all borrowings, which is the clue.

questions.stem: Where does the past participle go in a separable verb like „aufstehen“?
options: The ge- sits between the prefix and the stem
The ge- goes before the prefix
questions.explanation: „Aufgestanden“ — the ge- slots inside. It looks strange and is entirely regular.

questions.stem: Which verbs take „sein“ in the perfect tense?
options: Verbs of movement and change of state
questions.explanation: Gehen, fahren, kommen, bleiben and sein itself. „Bleiben“ is the one that breaks the movement rule and has to be memorised.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I stayed at home'?
questions.explanation: „Bleiben“ takes „sein“ despite no movement at all, and its participle is strong.

questions.stem: What does the imperfect of „haben“ look like for „ich“?
questions.explanation: „Ich hatte“ is the imperfect. „Hätte“ with an umlaut is the subjunctive, meaning 'would have'.

questions.stem: Which tense do Germans use for „sein“, „haben“ and the modals in speech?
questions.explanation: „Ich war“ and „ich hatte“ rather than „ich bin gewesen“. Every other verb prefers the perfect in conversation.

questions.stem: What is the imperfect of „gehen“ for „er“?
questions.explanation: Strong verbs change their stem and take no ending in the ich and er forms of the imperfect: ich ging, er ging.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'when I was ten, we lived in Berlin'?
options: Wann ich zehn war, wohnten wir in Berlin
Als ich zehn war, wohnten wir in Berlin
Wenn ich zehn war, wohnten wir in Berlin
Als ich war zehn, wohnten wir in Berlin
questions.explanation: „Als“ is for a single stretch of past time, „wenn“ for repeated or future time, and „wann“ only in questions.

questions.stem: What is the difference between „wenn“ and „als“?
options: They are interchangeable in the past
Als is for one past occasion, wenn for repeated ones
Als is formal and wenn is informal
Wenn is only used in questions
questions.explanation: „Immer wenn ich dort war“ — whenever. „Als ich dort war“ — that one time. English uses 'when' for both.

questions.stem: What ending does an adjective take after „der“ in the nominative?
questions.explanation: „Der große Mann“ — when the article already shows the case and gender, the adjective takes the weak ending -e.

questions.stem: What ending does an adjective take after „ein“ before a masculine noun?
questions.explanation: „Ein großer Mann“ — „ein“ does not show the gender, so the adjective has to, taking the ending the article would have had.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct adjective ending?
questions.explanation: After a definite article in the accusative, the adjective takes -en. All adjective endings in the plural and most in the accusative do.

questions.stem: What happens to adjective endings with no article at all?
options: The noun takes the ending instead
The adjective takes the article's ending
questions.explanation: „Guter Wein“ — with nothing in front, the adjective carries the full signal. This is why menus and headlines look so different.

questions.stem: Which case does „wegen“ take?
questions.explanation: Wegen, trotz, während and statt take the genitive in writing, though spoken German often uses the dative instead.

questions.stem: What is the genitive of „der Mann“?
questions.explanation: Masculine and neuter take „des“ and add -s or -es to the noun. Feminine and plural take „der“ and leave the noun alone.

questions.stem: How does German usually show possession in speech?
questions.explanation: „Das Auto von meinem Bruder“ rather than „meines Bruders Auto“. The genitive survives in writing and formal speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the man to whom I gave the book'?
options: Der Mann, den ich das Buch gegeben habe
Der Mann, der ich das Buch gegeben habe
Der Mann, dessen ich das Buch gegeben habe
Der Mann, dem ich das Buch gegeben habe
questions.explanation: A relative pronoun takes its case from its job in the relative clause, so an indirect object takes the dative „dem“.

questions.stem: Where does the verb go in a relative clause?
questions.explanation: Relative clauses are subordinate, so the verb goes last and a comma marks the boundary.

questions.stem: Which relative pronoun is used for a neuter noun in the nominative?
questions.explanation: Relative pronouns look like the definite article in most positions, which is why the case has to be worked out rather than guessed.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I know a man who speaks five languages'?
options: Ich kenne einen Mann, der fünf Sprachen spricht
Ich kenne einen Mann, den fünf Sprachen spricht
Ich kenne einen Mann, der spricht fünf Sprachen
Ich weiß einen Mann, der fünf Sprachen spricht
questions.explanation: The man is the subject of the relative clause, so „der“; the verb goes to the end; and knowing a person takes „kennen“.

questions.stem: What does „würde“ plus an infinitive express?
questions.explanation: „Ich würde gern fahren“ is the everyday conditional. A few common verbs have their own form instead: hätte, wäre, könnte, möchte.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'if I had time, I would read more'?
options: Wenn ich hätte Zeit, würde ich mehr lesen
Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mehr lesen
Wenn ich Zeit habe, würde ich mehr lesen
Wenn ich Zeit hätte, werde ich mehr lesen
questions.explanation: Both halves go conditional, the „wenn“ clause sends its verb to the end, and the main clause keeps the verb second.

questions.stem: What is the subjunctive form of „sein“ for „ich“?
questions.explanation: „Ich wäre“ means 'I would be'. The umlaut is the only thing separating it from the imperfect „war“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I should have studied more'?
questions.explanation: A modal in the perfect uses a double infinitive at the end rather than a participle. The word order is fixed and looks wrong until it is learnt.

questions.stem: Which modal means 'to be supposed to'?
questions.explanation: „Sollen“ carries an obligation placed on you by someone else. „Müssen“ is a harder necessity.

questions.stem: What does „nicht müssen“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Du musst nicht“ means you need not. 'Must not' is „du darfst nicht“, and the mix-up matters.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'you are not allowed to smoke here'?
questions.explanation: Permission is „dürfen“. „Müssen“ would say you do not have to, which is a different sign altogether.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the future tense correctly?
options: Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren
Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahre
Ich will morgen nach Berlin fahren
Ich werde morgen nach Berlin gefahren
questions.explanation: „Werden“ conjugated, infinitive at the end. „Wollen“ means want, not will, which is a false friend worth watching.

questions.stem: Why does German often use the present for future events?
options: A time expression makes the future clear
The future tense is reserved for formal writing
Werden cannot be used with a time expression
The present is compulsory after any time word
questions.explanation: „Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin“ is entirely normal. „Werden“ is kept for emphasis or when nothing else marks the time.

questions.stem: What does the passive „wird gebaut“ mean?
questions.explanation: The passive is „werden“ plus a past participle. Here the present of „werden“ gives a present passive.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary forms the German passive?
questions.explanation: „Das Haus wird gebaut“. Using „sein“ instead describes a finished state: „das Haus ist gebaut“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the house was built in 1900'?
questions.explanation: The imperfect of „werden“ is „wurde“, which carries the past passive.

questions.stem: What does „man“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Man sagt“ — they say. German often uses „man“ where English would reach for a passive.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids the passive the way German often does?
questions.explanation: All four are grammatical. „Man“ with an active verb is the everyday choice, exactly as „on“ is in French.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been living here for three years'?
options: Ich habe seit drei Jahren hier gewohnt
Ich wohnte seit drei Jahren hier
Ich werde seit drei Jahren hier wohnen
Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier
questions.explanation: „Seit“ with something still true takes the present tense, and „seit“ takes the dative, so the plural adds -n.

questions.stem: Which case follows „seit“?
questions.explanation: „Seit“ belongs to the always-dative group with mit, nach, aus, bei, von and zu.

questions.stem: What is the difference between „nach“ and „zu“ for going somewhere?
options: Nach is the formal word and zu the everyday one
Zu is used only when transport is mentioned
Nach is used only with a past tense verb
Nach is for towns, zu is for people and buildings
questions.explanation: „Nach Berlin“ but „zum Arzt“. „Nach Hause“ is the fixed exception that breaks the pattern.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going to the doctor'?
questions.explanation: „Zu“ plus „dem“ contracts to „zum“. With a feminine noun it would be „zur“.

questions.stem: Which contraction is correct for „in dem“?
questions.explanation: „In dem“ gives „im“ and „in das“ gives „ins“. The dative one describes being there, the accusative one going there.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am interested in music'?
questions.explanation: „Sich interessieren für“ is reflexive and takes the accusative. The preposition has to be learnt with the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am looking forward to the holidays'?
options: Ich freue mich für die Ferien
Ich freue mich auf die Ferien
Ich freue mich über die Ferien
questions.explanation: „Sich freuen auf“ looks forward; „sich freuen über“ is pleased about something that has already happened.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'he asked me whether I was coming'?
options: Er hat mich gefragt, wenn ich komme
Er hat mich gefragt, ob komme ich
Er hat mich gefragt, dass ich komme
Er hat mich gefragt, ob ich komme
questions.explanation: „Ob“ is 'whether' and is subordinating, so the verb goes to the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'although it was raining, we went out'?
options: Obwohl regnete es, sind wir ausgegangen
Obwohl es regnete, wir sind ausgegangen
Obwohl es regnete, sind ausgegangen wir
Obwohl es regnete, sind wir ausgegangen
questions.explanation: „Obwohl“ sends its verb to the end. The main clause then starts with the verb, because the whole subordinate clause counts as first position.

questions.stem: In „Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett“, why does „gehe“ come first in the second clause?
options: The comma resets the word order
The whole first clause fills position one
questions.explanation: Verb-second counts the subordinate clause as a single unit, so the main verb follows it immediately.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have to go now'?
questions.explanation: A modal takes a bare infinitive with no „zu“, and the infinitive waits at the end.

questions.stem: When does an infinitive take „zu“ in German?
options: After most verbs other than the modals
Only when the sentence is a question
Only when the main verb is in the past
questions.explanation: „Ich hoffe, dich zu sehen“. Modals, „lassen“ and verbs of perception take a bare infinitive instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'in order to learn German'?
questions.explanation: „Um ... zu“ is the purpose frame. The „zu“ sits immediately before the infinitive at the end.

questions.stem: What is the superlative of „gut“?
questions.explanation: Gut, besser, am besten — irregular throughout, like good, better, best.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she speaks German better than me'?
options: Sie spricht gut Deutsch als ich
Sie spricht mehr gut Deutsch als ich
Sie spricht besser Deutsch als ich
Sie spricht besser Deutsch wie ich
questions.explanation: „Als“ makes the comparison and „besser“ is the irregular comparative. „Wie“ is used for 'as ... as', not for 'than'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'as tall as'?
questions.explanation: Equality uses „so ... wie“ and inequality uses „als“. Mixing the two is the commonest comparative error.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'nobody was there'?
questions.explanation: „Niemand“ is a pronoun and takes a singular verb. „Kein“ has to sit in front of a noun.

questions.stem: What does „etwas“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Etwas“ is something, „nichts“ nothing, „alles“ everything and „jemand“ someone.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I do not like it at all'?
questions.explanation: „Gefallen“ turns the sentence round: the thing pleases the person, who sits in the dative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'my leg hurts'?
questions.explanation: „Wehtun“ puts the person in the dative and the body part as the subject, which is why the verb agrees with the leg.

questions.stem: Which sentence reports 'he said he was tired' as written German does?
options: Er sagte, dass er müde sein
Er sagte, dass ist er müde
Er sagte, dass er müde sei
questions.explanation: Reported speech in writing takes Konjunktiv I — „sei“ — which marks the words as someone else's. In speech you would hear the indicative „dass er müde ist“ instead, which is why the question asks for writing.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the more I practise, the better I speak'?
options: Je mehr ich übe, desto besser spreche ich
Je mehr ich übe, desto besser ich spreche
Mehr ich übe, desto besser spreche ich
Je mehr übe ich, desto besser spreche ich
questions.explanation: „Je ... desto“ sends the first verb to the end and keeps the second in position two. It is a fixed frame worth learning whole.
